items.title: Les Emirats arabes unis suspendent les vols des compagnies aériennes iraniennes
items.description: Les Émirats ont confirmé, jeudi, la suspension de tous les vols des compagnies aériennes iraniennes jusqu'à nouvel ordre. Une trentaine de compagnies aériennes iraniennes sont concernées. Les Emirats arabes unis ont suspendu jeudi tous les vols de compagnies iraniennes. « L'Autorité générale de l'aviation civile a annoncé la suspension de tous les vols opérés par des compagnies iraniennes vers et depuis les Emirats arabes unis, à compter d'aujourd'hui (…) et ce jusqu'à nouvel ordre », a indiqué un communiqué publié par l'agence de presse officielle WAM. Dubaï était la plus importante destination au Moyen-Orient pour les compagnies iraniennes avec plusieurs vols par jour depuis l'Iran. Les compagnies iraniennes utilisaient souvent les aéroports émiratis pour faire escale pour d'autres vols. Pour rappel, les Etats-Unis ont placé sous sanctions début septembre l'ensemble du secteur aérien de l'Iran et ont exhorté les entreprises étrangères à ne pas leur prêter assistance, par exemple en cessant le ravitaillement en kérosène des avions iraniens. Washington a donné jusqu'au 23 septembre pour que les entreprises se mettent en conformité. The post Les Emirats arabes unis suspendent les vols des compagnies aériennes iraniennes appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: The diplomacy of politics: The eighty first UNGA and impunity, by Owei Lakemfa
items.description: The United Nations General Assembly, UNGA is the global platform for all countries. So, no country can bar another speaking from its podium. But the United States, US at the on-going UNGA decided that the voice of the Palestinian State will not be heard. Only that of the State of Israel would be permitted. It therefore denied Palestinian Authority, PA, President Mahmoud Abbas an entry visa into the US, effectively barring a Head of State from attending UNGA. The US decided to illegally bar the Palestinian state from UNGA for having the nerve to take legal actions against Israel at the International Court of Justice, ICJ and the International Criminal Court, ICC. The Palestinian Case at these courts challenge the legality of Israel’s occupation of Gaza and the West Bank; its settlement policies under which Palestinian lands are stolen and given out to illegal Israeli settlers, and gross violations of international treaties and humanitarian law. A second reason US gave is that the PA rather than abandon its citizens convicted by the opaque Israeli courts, continues to provide financial stipends to their families. To the US, this amounts to the PA glorifying or supporting terrorism. The ICC in investigating war crimes and crimes against humanity perpetuated by the Israeli regime against the Palestinian people, had on November 21, 2024 issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the its former Minister of Defence, Yoav Gallant. So, essentially, the US is sitting on appeal against the ICC decision and is in a retaliatory mode against the Palestinians. But the US action in denying President Abass and the Palestinian delegation visa to attend UNGA, is a gross violation of the UN-USA Headquarters Agreement signed on June 26, 1947, and approved by UNGA on October 31, 1947. The Agreement signed by then UN Secretary-General Trygve LIE and, former US Secretary of State George C. Marshall, provides under Article IV Sections 11,12, and 13 that regardless of bilateral relations, the US would issue visas to State delegations and UN representatives promptly and without charge. It provides under Section 11 that: “The federal, state or local authorities of the United States shall not impose any impediments to transit to or from the headquarters district…” for these officials. Sections 12 and 13 further stated that: “The provisions of Section 11 shall be applicable irrespective of the relations existing between the Governments of the persons referred to in that section and the Government of the United States.” “Laws and regulations in force in the United States regarding the entry of aliens shall not be applied in such manner as to interfere with the privileges referred to in Section 11. When visas are required for persons referred to in that section, they shall be granted without charge and as promptly as possible.” For UNGA, this was not the time to discuss the US violating the Agreement or, hear demands that the UN headquarters be moved to a more receptive country. What was important was to hear him. It was therefore proposed that Abass should be heard via video link. But even this, irked the US which staked his reputation by urging UNGA not to accept this minimum compromise. US Deputy Ambassador to the UN Tammy Bruce argued that: “If the PA wants to be treated as a partner, it must stop subsidizing terror and stop using diplomatic theater as a substitute for serious governance.” The American representative added: “We will not relent on our insistence that the Palestinian Authority and the PLO [Palestine Liberation Organisation] completely and unequivocally renounce terrorism. They have not yet done so.” The matter was put to vote and 152 countries voted for the resolution while only three countries voted for the US position. These were Paraguay, the US itself and its partner, Israel. Four abstained; Panama, Honduras, Peru and Colombia. Thus, the world sat and listened to the Palestinian leader who described the Israeli war in the Palestine as genocide and urged humanity to act and, not fold its arms. He demanded that the Israeli attacks and military occupation of the Palestine be brought to an end. Abass posited that a permanent solution should be effected whereby the Israelis and Palestinians would live in their various countries with guaranteed security and, in peace. In contrast to the treatment meted out to President Abass, US welcomed Prime Minister Netanyahu. But UNGA did not welcome him. When he began to speak, 77 Delegations walked out rather than listen to a man who has an international warrant of arrest hanging round his neck. He had no choice but to address a virtually empty hall. But he is not a man capable of reading a simple situation. Rather than present his country’s case, he ranted how Israel and its allies have been eliminating people and destroying countries: “Half the Houthi leadership in Yemen – gone. Yahya Sinwar in Gaza – gone. Hassan Nasrallah in Lebanon – gone. The Assad regime in Syria – gone. Those Militias in Iraq? Well, they’re still deterred. And their leaders, if they attack Israel, will also be gone. And for Iran’s top military commanders and its top nuclear scientists… Well, they’re gone too.” When President Trump arrived the UN Headquarters on Tuesday September 22, 2026 it was like a theatre. He had banned the CNN from the White House and might have been oblivious of the fact that the UN is not US territory , so his ban had no effect there. He told the news channel: “I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me. You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to cover me” CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins replied: “The United Nations allowed us in, sir.” The response was clear; Trump did not call the shots in the UN. Playing God, Trump told UNGA about his assumed choices on Iran: “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic? ….Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” But Iran is no country to bully or, backdown. Its President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country will fight to its last breath: “The United States president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism,” “Are we the sources of instability? We only seek to live independently,” “We are the ones who cause instability? Those who are committing terrorism and committing crimes, are they the protectors of peace and stability?” On the side lines, the US and Iran held a three-hour meeting. Perhaps it is an admission that impunity and bullying will ultimately, not pay. The post The diplomacy of politics: The eighty first UNGA and impunity, by Owei Lakemfa appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 2027: Elections must be decided at polls, not courts — Onaiyekan, Osigwe
items.description: ***Idris, Achebe, Utomi, Anaba, Mbah, others chart way forward for Nigeria, democracy, media ***Demand reforms as editors warn against AI-driven electoral misinformation By Anayo Okoli, Dennis Agbo & Chinedu Adonu ENUGU — THE judiciary and its increasingly prominent role in determining the outcome of Nigerian elections came under intense scrutiny at the 22nd All Nigeria Editors Conference, ANEC, in Enugu, yesterday, with leading voices warning that democracy was weakened when the courts become the arena in which electoral victories were finally decided. From the keynote address by Catholic Archbishop Emeritus of Abuja, John Cardinal Onaiyekan, to the interventions of former Nigerian Bar Association President, Mazi Afam Osigwe, SAN, and political economist, Prof. Patrick Utomi, the conference repeatedly returned to one troubling question: Should the courts be deciding who governs Nigerians after voters have supposedly made that decision at the ballot box? The question acquired particular urgency against the background of the 2027 general elections and concerns over declining public confidence in electoral institutions. The conference, organised by the Nigerian Guild of Editors, NGE, was held under the theme, “The Ballot, the Media and the Task of Keeping Democracy Alive,” with the sub-theme, “When Lies Look Real: Detecting and Debunking AI Misinformation Before, During, and After Elections.” Other key personalities, who spoke at the well-attended event included President of NGE and Editor of Vanguard Newspapers, Mr Eze Anaba; Minister of Information, Mohammed Idris; Obi of Onitsha, Igwe Alfred Achebe; and governor of Enugu State, Dr Peter Mbah. The conference was also attended by Governor Umar Namadi of Jigawa State; Deputy Governor of Enugu State, Ifeanyi Osisi; Vanguard publisher, Uncle Sam Amuka; former governor of Ogun State, Aremo Olusegun Osoba; and Information Minister, who was represented by Ali. M Ali, the MD of NAN, Others include Prof. Auwal Yadudu, SAN; Chief Onyema Ugochukwu; Tunde Rahman; Prof. Stella Ọkunna, and INEC chairman, Joash Amupitan, who was represented by Enugu REC, Chukwuemeka Chukwu. Elections being determined in courts, not at polls Delivering the keynote address, Onaiyekan said democracy was ultimately about government serving the people, adding that elections should provide the mechanism through which people were elected. He expressed concern that Nigeria’s electoral system had evolved into one in which the courts increasingly became the final battleground for political contests. According to him, the judiciary was originally intended to adjudicate disputes arising from elections, not to become the institution through which electoral victories were effectively determined. “The judiciary is supposed to be the last stage in the electoral process. It should be stressed that the judiciary is not to determine elections about who wins, but rather to adjudicate disputes when they arise,” he said. He argued that if elections were properly conducted, there should be little need for prolonged litigation. “If elections were well conducted, there ought not to be any need for judicial cases. The tribunals were supposed to be there just in case.” But, according to him, Nigeria’s recent experience had produced an uncomfortable reversal. Onaiyekan said: “Our experience in the recent past has almost become that we have been witnessing a situation where our elections are being determined not at the polls, but in the courts by the tribunals.’’ He said the development had created opportunities for highly paid lawyers to exploit technicalities in prolonged legal battles. “This gives a field day for high-class lawyers with high-level fees, doing their best to manipulate issues on technicalities,” he said. The Cardinal also expressed concern over allegations of unjust judgments in election tribunals, saying such perceptions had damaged public confidence in one of the country’s most important institutions. “There are allegations that are difficult to deny of unjust judgments by some judges in election tribunals,” he said, adding that the performance of the judiciary in recent elections had “seriously dented the image of this hallowed institution.” He said efforts must be made to restore public trust in the courts. Among others, Onaiyekan, who urged the media to resist pressure and uphold democracy, called for electoral reforms, independent INEC, and for a candidate to score at least 50 per cent of votes cast to be declared winner of a presidential election. Onaiyekan’s seven-point reform agenda Onaiyekan proposed a series of reforms aimed at reducing the dependence of Nigeria’s electoral system on post-election litigation. Among them was the creation of a special election tribunal dedicated exclusively to electoral cases and required to dispose of petitions within a defined period. While arguing that that election disputes should be resolved before elected officials assumed office, the cleric said: “More seriously, we must do all that is necessary to dispose of all tribunal cases before swearing in any candidate.’’ He questioned the fairness of a system in which a declared winner assumed office and then used the machinery and resources of government to defend the victory in court against an opponent. “A situation where a candidate has been declared a president still going to tribunal to defend his position using state means and state resources to defend himself against his opponents is not serious as far as natural justice is concerned,” he said. Onaiyekan further argued that ordinary voters should have a greater role in electoral litigation. Under the present system, he noted, candidates were generally the principal parties with the legal standing to challenge election results. But the people who actually cast the votes, he argued, should not be completely excluded from the legal process where they believed their votes were improperly counted. “We who cast the votes and whose votes are at stake have no room to complain. This must change,” he said. He also proposed a review of the process for appointing INEC leadership, arguing that electoral commissioners should not be overly dependent on political authorities who might themselves be contestants in elections. Onaiyekan questioned how genuinely independent the commission could be when its leadership structure was closely connected to the executive arm of government. The cleric, who urged Nigerians not to abandon the democratic ideal because of its imperfections, acknowledged that democracy was difficult to practise but argued that Nigeria could not use that difficulty as an excuse for accepting defective institutions. “The ultimate objective is to install a government that is freely chosen by the people and that works for the common good of the people,” he said. He also stressed the importance of the character of those who emerge as leaders, saying “they must be persons with a minimum of social values and character: honesty, concern for the common good of citizens as priority of governance, absolute respect for the rule of just laws.’’ For the Nigerian media, the challenge ahead, he noted, was therefore larger than reporting an election. According to him, it is the challenge of protecting the information upon which citizens make electoral choices, scrutinising those who exercise public power, reporting the work of electoral institutions and courts accurately, and ensuring that neither political propaganda nor technological deception was allowed to become a substitute for truth. He said the 2027 election would ultimately be decided through votes but noted that the credibility of those votes would depend heavily on whether Nigerians could trust the institutions that counted them, the courts that adjudicated disputes over them, and the media that told the public what happened. Osigwe speaks Onaiyekan’s concern was amplified by the immediate past president of NBA, Osigwe, who told editors that Nigeria had become one of the countries with a high number of election petitions. Speaking on “Election Petition in the Digital Age: Independence, Evidence, BVAS,” the former NBA president said the increasing involvement of the courts in electoral contests had raised fundamental questions about whether elections were being determined by voters or through litigation. “I see that Nigeria is one of the countries with the highest number of election petitions, and all because the courts are very frequently involved in determining either the outcome or who won,” Osigwe said. He recalled that a judge had previously described the development as the “judicialisation of the electoral process.” For Osigwe, the expression captures a growing problem in which electoral disputes move from polling units to courtrooms, transforming judges into key actors in determining the political fate of candidates. “All too often, the courts are merely called in to give direction on issues of procedure,” he said. He identified the difficulty of proving electoral violations as one factor driving litigation, arguing that the way elections were conducted and the limited time available for petitioners to establish their cases had made the judicial process even more complicated. He also questioned aspects of the evidential framework governing election petitions, particularly where technology, such as the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System, BVAS, and the INEC Result Viewing Portal, IReV, was involved. He argued that technological systems introduced to improve electoral transparency should not become additional obstacles for candidates seeking to establish alleged irregularities. Technology, he maintained, should make elections more transparent rather than make it harder for petitioners to prove what happened at polling units. He also questioned the treatment of subpoenaed evidence in election petitions, particularly documents which petitioners might not have been able to obtain before filing their cases. On IReV, Osigwe argued that the platform should receive meaningful evidential recognition in election litigation, even if it was not treated as the primary evidence of election results. His concerns extended to proposed legal provisions which, according to him, can prevent non-compliance with INEC regulations and guidelines from constituting grounds for challenging an election. He argued that where INEC was empowered to make regulations and guidelines, compliance with such rules should have consequences for the credibility of the electoral process. The central issue, he said, was whether a person should be declared the winner of an election when questions remained about whether the process leading to that declaration complied with the rules. ‘Go to court’ culture Osigwe also took aim at the familiar political expression, “Go to court,” which is often directed at defeated candidates after disputed elections. He questioned what such statements communicated about confidence in the electoral justice system. For him, the phrase can create the impression that political actors already understood the limitations confronting those who seek judicial redress. The former NBA president also raised concerns about public perceptions of corruption within the judiciary, while making clear that he was not personally vouching for allegations of bribery against judges. He said the widespread perception that litigants might have to pay for favourable judicial outcomes was itself damaging to confidence in the justice system. The issue, according to him, is particularly sensitive because the judiciary represents the final institutional avenue for candidates and citizens who believe that an election has been conducted improperly. He noted that if citizens lose confidence in that avenue, the consequences extend beyond individual election petitions to the legitimacy of the democratic process itself. Osigwe similarly raised questions about public confidence in the electoral commission, particularly the process through which its officials were appointed. ‘’The concern is not merely institutional. Where the electoral umpire is perceived as lacking independence, the credibility of election results can be affected even before disputes reach the courts. That, in turn, increases the likelihood of litigation and places additional pressure on the judiciary,’’ Osigwe added. The ballot versus the courtroom On his part, President of the Nigerian Guild of Editors, Eze Anaba, captured the relationship between the ballot and the judiciary when he said the credibility of elections must be protected, so courts would not have to replace citizens in determining who represented them. “The credibility of the ballot must be protected so that the courts do not have to replace the citizenry in determining who should represent the people,” Anaba said. He said voters could only make informed choices when they had access to credible information and were free from intimidation and undue influence. For Anaba, therefore, the media’s responsibility begins long before election day. He said editors must provide citizens with information that allowed them to assess candidates, policies and government performance without being manipulated by political propaganda or misinformation. AI opens another battlefield – Idris But as Nigeria approaches another election cycle, the traditional problems of electoral politics are being compounded by a new technological threat: artificial intelligence. The Minister of Information and National Orientation, Mohammed Idris, who was represented at the conference by the Managing Director of the News Agency of Nigeria, Ali M. Ali, warned that AI-generated misinformation could create an entirely new environment in which fabricated events appeared real. He said artificial intelligence had made it possible to create convincing photographs, videos, audio recordings and documents that had never existed. “A false statement can be produced in the voice of a public official. A fabricated video can be circulated within minutes. An old photograph can be presented as a current event,” Idris said. The danger, he warned, was not only that people might believe falsehoods, but that they could eventually lose confidence in everything they saw or heard. The minister urged editors to make verification a permanent newsroom culture. He challenged journalists to ask basic questions, including who said it? What is the evidence? When was the photograph taken? Is the video original? Has the source been independently verified? Does the headline reflect the story? Before publication. He also urged journalists to distinguish clearly between fact, allegation and opinion. “The job of a professional journalist is not to amplify every claim simply because it is politically attractive. The job is to establish what is true, provide context and allow citizens to make their own judgments,” he said. Achebe: ‘When the mirror is cracked’ Chairman of the conference and Obi of Onitsha, HRH Igwe Alfred Nnaemeka Achebe, warned that AI-generated misinformation could distort the very information upon which citizens based electoral decisions. He said a voice could be fabricated to sound exactly like a governor, while a video could place a political candidate at an event that never happened. “A voice that sounds exactly like a governor can now say what he never said. A video can place a candidate where he never was,” Achebe said. He expressed particular concern about the speed with which false information could travel through WhatsApp groups, family networks, town unions and community platforms. Achebe, who urged journalists to place verification above speed, said: “The discipline of pausing to ask, ‘how do I know that this is true?’ must become as instinctive as the instinct to rush to publish used to be.’’ He proposed the creation of a joint Election Rapid Response Desk involving newsrooms that could identify, verify and debunk viral falsehoods before they spread widely. Using a striking metaphor, Achebe described the ballot as the citizen’s voice and the media as the mirror through which the citizen sees the world. “When the mirror is cracked, or worse, deliberately distorted, the citizen no longer votes from truth, but votes from illusion,” he said. Utomi’s warning For Utomi, the consequences of a failing electoral system go beyond elections. He warned that weak institutions could ultimately undermine the stability and survival of the country. The political economist said elections were essential to legitimising government and building institutions. “If the people are convinced that there is no point, what is an election? Imagine the amount of money we waste to have elections that are totally meaningless because they do not legitimise anybody,” he said. Utomi argued that strong institutions create predictable rules and reduce uncertainty. But when abnormal practices became normalised, he said, the cost of doing business rises and citizens gradually lose faith in legitimate avenues for resolving grievances. “What has happened to us, unfortunately, is because the abnormal has become so accepted that the transaction costs of engaging in Nigeria are such that we are only heading in one direction — ultimate collapse,” he warned. He said the media had a critical responsibility in preventing such institutional decay. Press, govt must meet at point of truth – Mbah In his remarks, Enugu State governor, Peter Mbah, challenged Nigerian journalists to deepen investigative journalism and relentlessly establish facts in the face of growing artificial intelligence-generated misinformation capable of making falsehoods appear real. He said the press and government might have different responsibilities but must ultimately serve the same purpose — the interest of the Nigerian people. The governor, who joked that the gathering offered a temporary “ceasefire” between government and the media, said: “Government must be transparent about what it is doing and be accountable for the results. The press must establish the facts and report the truth.” He urged journalists not to allow investigative journalism become a lost art, stressing that newsrooms must be willing to distinguish between information that merely generated attention and issues the public genuinely needed to know. According to him, “rigorous journalism is not about finding evidence to support a position already taken, nor should it become another arena for political grandstanding.” Mbah also used the occasion to highlight his administration’s development programmes, saying his government was seeking to transform Enugu into an economic gateway for the South-East, one of Nigeria’s top three states by GDP and a national leader in human development and quality of life. He listed more than 1,500 kilometres of roads constructed or reconstructed, over 7,000 classrooms delivered, Smart Green Schools and Type-2 primary healthcare centres across the 260 electoral wards, restoration of water supply in Enugu metropolis, new transport terminals, CNG buses and the revival of dormant industries. He also cited the operations of Enugu Air and the development of Enugu Smart City as part of the transformation agenda. The governor said the state had enjoyed strong collaboration with President Bola Tinubu and the federal government, particularly through increased support to states and interventions in roads, aviation, energy and regional development. He said the concessioning of Akanu Ibiam International Airport would further strengthen Enugu’s position as a gateway to the South-East. Mbah, however, acknowledged that there was still much work to be done, urging the visiting editors to move beyond official claims and independently assess the changes taking place across the state. items.title: Rising fuel prices and insensitivity to the peoples’ plight, by Adekunle Adekoya
items.description: AGAIN, I am still on the matter of rising prices of fuel energy, particularly petrol, which is heading towards N1,500, automotive gas oil, AGO or diesel, which is heading towards N2,000, and cooking gas, which is selling at above N22,000 for a 12.5 kilogramme cylinder. That sold for N3,500 BC, Before Change in 2015. It is trite to begin to repeat how the rising prices of these fuels have inflicted a cost of living crisis on all of us. There are very few Nigerians left who are able to save for the rainy day; almost all of us spend everything we earn on food, transportation, and accommodation. As things stand, the more fortunate among us are those with kongi (extremely strong) make-up, who don’t fall sick. It now costs a fortune to treat ordinary malaria or typhoid fever. If you come down with anything more serious than that, you’d probably need crowd-funding to meet healthcare costs. As if these are normal, some not so normal people keep defending the deleterious effects of these policies as if they live in outer space where things are cheaper and only fly in to work here. Many of them, particularly government appointees, keep using metrics from saner climes to explain why we should suffocate to death. But we must remind them that they are damned wrong; as the conditions are not the same at all. The only thing common to us and the countries they are fond of referring to is that we also have crude oil. The major difference between us and these countries is what their leaders used their oil wealth to achieve, versus what could not be done here. Let’s take some samplers: As at now one litre of fuel in Iran costs the equivalent of N38. In Lybya, one litre of fuel sells at the equivalent of N32. Saudi Arabia, where both leaders and followers troop to for pilgrimage, one litre sells at the equivalent of N823. Comparatively, minimum wage in Iran is the equivalent of N165,000, while in Libya it is about N210,000. In Saudi Arabia, minimum wage is the equivalent of N1.4 million. We all know how much minimum wage is here, comparatively, a paltry N70,000. Let’s take it further: minimumwage in Iran will buy 4,342 litres and in Libya will buy 6,562 litres. In Saudi Arabia, the minimum wage will buy 1,700 litres. All four countries referred to here, alongside Nigeria are all oil producing nations. In the four countries aforementioned, there is no road uncompleted like the East-West Road. Also, they don’t have a road like the Benin By-Pass on which travelers spend three days for a journey that should take no more than six hours. In those countries too, their citizens do not suffer electric power outages as we do here; neither do they routinely go abroad for medical treatment. Schools are running, hospitals have drugs and doctors. While they each have issues they are contending with, they have managed successfully to insulate the masses of their people from the deleterious effects of these issues. Here, we remain exposed to everything. It is worth repeating that despite the damages suffered by Iran as a result of the conflict with US/Israel, life is still predictable for most Iranians. Despite fears of aerial bombings and rocket as well as drone attacks, children are going to school and hospitals continue to function normally. Right now, nobody knows who is in charge of Libya since Gaddafi was ousted and killed. But the joke is on Nigeria and her peoples as thousands of Nigerians are working in that country virtually as slaves. Have you heard that the daughter of the woman next door, who has not been seen in the neighborhood for months is now a “shagallah” in Libya, or other Arabian Emirates like Omañ, or Kuwait? Or that many more of our youths are planning to “japa” to these countries to b come shagallah? I am not saying all the issues that cumulated to what we are seeing today began with the current administration. No. The issue is that this government campaigned with the Renewed Hope slogan. From day one, May 29, 2023, it was anything but renewed hope. In fact, most Nigerians are currently wallowing in renewed hopelessness. Insecurity has worsened, and the economy is now working in favour of the common man. That is the issue. What we hoped to see since May 29,2023 was redoubled efforts to improve our lot, not what we are going through now, which is the reverse of what we hoped for This is what triggered the promise of a section of the political class to return to subsidy if it wins next year’s election. Whether that was wise or not is not the issue at the moment; what is clear is that we, the people of Nigeria need lifelines, and now. The Almighty US, with the largest economy in the world, operates 14 different types of subsidies. Why should ours be different? Going forward, government and its leaders must stop being insensitive to our plight. In this election season, it is insouciant to continue carrying on as if all is normal. No, sirs; things are not normal with us and the ruling party and it’s cohorts must do everything possible to restore normalcy. No be so? TGIF. The post Rising fuel prices and insensitivity to the peoples’ plight, by Adekunle Adekoya appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 197% jump in drug arrests proof of stronger enforcement under NDC – Majority
items.description: The National Democratic Congress Majority Caucus in Parliament has called for stronger collaboration among security and law enforcement agencies to dismantle drug trafficking networks operating in Ghana. The Caucus, therefore, attributed the sharp increase in recent narcotics arrests and seizures to strategic reforms under the National Democratic Congress (NDC) administration. Addressing a press conference in Parliament House on Thursday, September, Mr James Agalga, the Majority Leader and NDC Member of Parliament (MP) for Builsa North, said the growing complexity of the narcotics trade required a coordinated national response involving institutions responsible for border security, intelligence, investigations, prosecution, port operations and asset recovery. “The Majority Caucus urges all security and law enforcement agencies, particularly the Narcotics Control Commission, the Ghana Police Service, the Ghana Immigration Service, the Ports and Harbours Authority and others, to increase cooperation and present one front to combat the emergence of drug networks in our country,” he said. Mr Agalga said no single institution had the capacity to tackle the entire drug trafficking chain alone, stressing that intelligence sharing and joint operations are critical. He said: “This is no job for any single agency. Profiling and screening, investigation, prosecution and asset recovery are all critical elements in the chain, and only when agencies are better coordinated, sharing intelligence and working together can Ghana really disrupt and dismantle networks that traffic narcotics. The Majority Caucus called for continued and concerted inter-agency cooperation as the bedrock of the nation’s struggle against the drug menace. The Majority Leader defended the government’s record in the fight against narcotics, citing enforcement data from the Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC). Mr Agalga disclosed that NACOC recorded 73 arrests nationwide in 2024, which was then its highest annual figure, but increased to 217 arrests across 165 cases in 2025. “In 2024, NACOC recorded 73 arrests nationwide. In 2025, NACOC enforcement operations produced 217 arrests across 165 cases, an increase of 197 per cent. So let’s compare the figures: 73 arrests versus 217 arrests. In percentage terms, we are looking at a 197 per cent increase,” he said. He said the 2025 performance was due to concrete institutional changes introduced by the government, including the expansion of NACOC’s District Commands from fewer than 10 to 77, extending its presence to all 16 regions. He added that stronger collaboration with the Ghana Police Service, National Intelligence Bureau, Ghana Immigration Service and the Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO) had supported intelligence-led operations. According to the Majority Leader, NACOC also seized 1,497.75 kilogrammes of narcotic substances in 2025 at an estimated street value of US$5.24 million, alongside 61,974 units of controlled substances, including pharmaceutical opiates and new psychoactive substances. Asset-based enforcement operations, he said, resulted in the seizure of GH¢6.93 million and US$440,382 in cash, as well as 19.72 kilogrammes of gold allegedly linked to suspected drug-money laundering. Mr Agalga said the government had also established a dedicated narcotics court to address fragmentation in the prosecution of drug cases and help close the gap between arrests and convictions. “The 2025 performance was due to the concrete institutional changes this government has put in place,” he emphasised.

items.title: Nigeria’s fertiliser use shortfall
items.description: Nigeria’s fertiliser paradox is becoming harder to ignore. The country now possesses fertiliser production capacity, yet farmers are applying nowhere near enough nutrients to unlock its agricultural potential. The Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security says national fertiliser consumption is about 18.6 kilogrammes per hectare, against the 50kg/ha benchmark associated with the 2006 Abuja Declaration. The Fertiliser Producers and Sellers Association of Nigeria (FEPSAN), using another measure, put application at 24kg/ha in March 2026. Either way, the shortfall is substantial. FAO-based data show Nigeria at 22.6kg/ha in 2020, falling to 18.0kg in 2021, 7.3kg in 2022 and 4.2kg in 2023. Differences between these figures reflect methodology but show that fertiliser deployment has not kept pace with agricultural needs. The International Fertiliser Development Centre (IFDC) recorded 79kg/ha in Zambia and 14.4kg/ha in Tanzania in 2020, illustrating how far national averages can diverge. ECOWAS has now adopted an ambition to triple fertiliser consumption and double agricultural production by 2035. For Nigeria, reaching 50kg/ha should be regarded as a minimum strategic benchmark, not an excuse for indiscriminate application. The appropriate rate must vary with crop, soil, climate and nutrient requirements. But a country seeking abundant food supplies from millions of hectares cannot remain at these levels. Higher, scientifically targeted use of mineral and organic nutrients, combined with improved seeds, irrigation, extension and mechanisation, is indispensable. Why is deployment so poor? Cost is a major factor. Fertiliser prices, transport expenses, foreign-exchange pressures, weak rural infrastructure and limited farm credit have made inputs unaffordable. Distribution is another: fertiliser may be produced in abundance but still fail to reach farmers on time. Weak extension services and inadequate soil testing further encourage inefficient or insufficient application. But the gravest obstacle is insecurity. Terrorists and bandits have occupied or rendered inaccessible forests, farmlands and rural corridors in parts of the North-East, North-West and North-Central food-basket zones. Farmers have been killed, kidnapped, taxed, threatened or driven from their fields. FAO reports that conflict is severely disrupting agricultural activity in key food-producing states and that more than 3.7 million Nigerians were internally displaced by early August 2026. The consequences are visible in the hunger stalking the land. Nearly 36.3 million people were estimated to face Crisis-level food insecurity or worse during the June–August 2026 lean season. Displacement destroys farming assets, labour and planting cycles, while reduced harvests tighten supplies and push prices upward. Government must therefore treat fertiliser and security policy as inseparable. The Federal and State Governments must act decisively and systematically to restore security across Nigeria, reclaim threatened farming communities, reopen productive land for cultivation and markets, and restore rural economic life safely. Without safe access to farms, no fertiliser programme can deliver food abundance. Only a secure Nigeria can feed its roughly 240 million people. Security is the foundation of food production. The post Nigeria’s fertiliser use shortfall appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Pezeshkian says Islamabad MoU still 'fully acceptable' to Iran, ready to take it forward: PM Shehbaz
items.description: NEW YORK: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said on Thursday that Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had told him the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was “fully acceptable” to Tehran even today and that they were “ready to take it forward”. The premier’s statement came after he held a “detailed” discussion with the Iranian president on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York. Earlier, a statement by the PM’s Office said that the premier stressed the importance of implementing the Islamabad MoU — a 14-point interim agreement signed between the US and Iran in June that gave a framework for ending the ongoing conflict — in the meeting. Pakistan had also signed the agreement as a mediator. The conflict, however, has since continued with sporadic strikes and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports, while Iran has maintained control over traffic through the strategic waterway. After PM Shehbaz met with Pezeshkian, he was asked by the media about the possibility of any progress on de-escalating the situation in the Middle East. The premier replied that Pakistan’s leadership united in its resolve to expedite the peace efforts under the Islamabad MoU. He also mentioned the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — two key waterways for the world’s oil fuel supply that have been affected by the conflict in the Middle East. “The current situation in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, and the provocative activities taking place there, require brotherly and friendly countries to work together to reduce tensions,” he stressed. “For this purpose, today I met the Iranian president, had a detailed meeting with him, and told him that restoring peace to the region is the need of the hour, a very important need,” he said. PM Shehbaz said Pakistan, as it had done in the past, would continue working for peace with Iran, which he described as a “brotherly” and neighbouring country. “I told him that Pakistan’s leadership, whether military or political, will, God willing, work together and continue its efforts to bring peace to the region,” he said. The premier further narrated that in his meeting with President Pezeshkian, the latter appreciated Pakistan’s efforts and reaffirmed Iran’s acceptance of the Islamabad MoU. “The Iranian president said the Islamabad MoU is still fully acceptable to us and they are ready to take it forward,” he added. The prime minister said Pakistan would continue working with friendly and brotherly countries to help reduce tensions and promote peace in the region. Earlier, the PMO statement said PM Shehbaz expressed “deep concern over the prolonged conflict and emphasised the need for restraint, de-escalation, and sustained diplomatic engagement to achieve lasting peace and stability in the region” in his meeting with Pezeshkian. “He also underscored the importance of implementing the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding and reaffirmed Pakistan’s readiness to continue playing sincere and constructive role in support of regional peace and stability,” the statement added. The two leaders discussed the evolving regional situation, with Pezeshkian appreciating Pakistan’s “principled diplomacy and concerted efforts for regional peace and security”, according to the statement. “Underlining the importance of maintaining regular consultations and close coordination to address the prevailing challenges and seize the opportunities, the two sides agreed to work for regional peace, security, and prosperity,” it said. Regarding bilateral ties, the two leaders reaffirmed the close and longstanding ties between Pakistan and Iran and underscored the need to further strengthen bilateral cooperation across all areas of mutual interest, it added. “The Iranian President also underscored the enduring strength of Pakistan-Iran relations, rooted in shared history, culture, and faith, and reaffirmed Tehran’s strong desire to further deepen multifaceted cooperation,” it said. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, and Special Assistant to the Prime Minister Tariq Fatemi were also present at the meeting, as well as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. During his interaction with the media, PM Shehbaz highlighted what he described as close cooperation between Pakistan’s political and military leadership, saying that this teamwork was contributing both to diplomatic efforts and economic stability. Asked whether he had taken the Iranian president into confidence about the Makkah Defence Alliance, the prime minister said, “Yes, this was discussed, and we did inform him.” Soon after the prime minister spoke, reporters asked Defence Minister Khawaja Asif whether Iran was on board on the Makkah accord. He said Pakistan had discussed the agreement with Iran, and that it could join the alliance in the future. The alliance’s member states, he said, were still in the process of setting up the accord’s secretariat, after which further details would be discussed. PM Shehbaz and Pezeshkian had previously held a meeting in Kyrgyzstan, on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Council of Heads of State meeting in August, during which they reaffirmed the close and longstanding ties between both countries. At the same time, PM Shehbaz had also stressed the importance of restraint and sustained diplomatic engagement to achieve lasting peace and stability in the region amid the US-Iran conflict. Thursday’s meeting with the Iranian president comes as Islamabad continues efforts to bring the United States and Iran back to the negotiating table regarding the war in the Middle East. Pezeshkian on Wednesday struck a defiant tone speaking at the UN for the first time since Washington and Israel launched an all-out war on his country, vowing Tehran would never “bend at the knee”. He made no reference to the talks to resolve the stalled war in his steely speech. However, the Iranian side earlier this week indicated its willingness to return to dialogue with the US to de-escalate tensions. The flexibility on the issue was indicated by the Iranian side in a meeting between Pezeshkian and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi during the latter’s visit to Tehran. Pakistan, meanwhile, has remained engaged in efforts to keep the diplomatic channel open. Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir has used his contacts with the US administration, while Pakistani officials have made repeated visits to Tehran. Diplomatic sources say Qatar is handling the immediate shuttle diplomacy between the US and Iran in New York, while Pakistan is working through a parallel channel with Tehran as regional efforts intensify to keep the latest diplomatic contacts from collapsing. The distinction has emerged from reporting by US and international media on the renewed US-Iran contacts around the United Nations General Assembly, with Qatar and Pakistan both involved in efforts to keep communication open between Washington and Tehran. PM Shehbaz is expected to address the UNGA on Friday.

items.title: Container city
items.description: EVEN after butchering local ecologies and evicting tens of thousands from their decades-old homes, they insist on calling it Islamabad the beautiful. It really ought to be called Container City. The federal capital — and its twin city, Rawalpindi — once again resembles a loading dock for cargo ships. And as always, we are told that besieging the twin cities is in the greater national interest. The fact that official definitions of the national interest are completely unrelated to popular sentiment is not a new quandary for the powers that be. But in comparison to almost every other dispensation in Pakistan’s history, this regime is not bothered with gaining even a modicum of consent from the people, having liberally deployed the big stick in the country’s core regions to match what has always been the historical norm in the peripheries. Barely veiled threats have been issued this time too, ‘violent groups’ warned against trying to enter Islamabad. There have been a series of pre-emptive strikes against anyone and everyone that the government designates a ‘security risk’. From Imran Khan’s elderly sisters to the president of the Islamabad street vendors’ association, the regime is intent on ensuring that it alienates even those who have no link to the PTI. Whether the latter’s ‘long march’ even materialises is irrelevant, because the optics of a heavily contained population is the real story. The container city, in fact, is a microcosm of the country at large. If you have a dissenting political opinion, you can be locked up, issued a Peca notice, or maybe even disappeared. To aspire to an economic situation beyond bare survival requires one to work longer and harder for slave wages — if you are amongst those from the army of unemployed that can actually find work. The container city is a microcosm of the country at large. It should not go unnoticed that Islamabad’s police officials have asked for Rs827 million to manage the yet-to-happen protests. Meanwhile, there is no suggestion that even a pittance of that sum will be allocated to upgrade facilities and quality of services in PIMS in the wake of the horrific fire which claimed the lives of 14 newborns. There is no pretence at play here, no meaningful hegemonic strategy. The only consistent and conscious interest of the regime is in the realm of geopolitics. But unlike authoritarian rule under Ayub, Zia and Musharraf, today’s rulers cannot count on a structural windfall due to favourable geopolitical winds. Aside from acquiring geostrategic rents from anti-communist Seato and Cento pacts, the Ayub regime actually had an industrial policy, cultivating something resembling a manufacturing sector and absorbing some labouring masses displaced from the agrarian sector. The 22 families, including emergent state profiteers, may have captured the major spoils, but there was some logic to the regime’s claim that a little wealth would eventually ‘trickle down’ to the masses. Even while presiding over de-industrialisation, Zia benefited from the Gulf remittances as well as big industrial investments made under the Bhutto dispensation, not to mention windfalls from the ‘Afghan jihad’. Musharraf came to power after industrial policy was definitively declared dead, but the dictatorship nevertheless benefited from post 9/11 remittances and ‘war on terror’ dollars. The current dispensation only secures fuel to keep government running the next day by extorting the masses through a levy, while its economic imagination is limited to FDI and a developmental logic revolving around resource grabs. It has shut down border trade with Afghanistan, which is a major supply of the everyday eco­­nomy. Mean­while, members of the Pakistani bourgeoisie itself lament its comp­rador character, the CEO of the Sentinel Group recently penn­ing a telling essay on ‘Pakistan’s missing multinationals’. To be sure, the rot extends much deeper than the present regime. The so-called ‘demographic dividend’ which has been hyped up for at least 15 years is, instead, a huge pressure cooker; neither the state nor the private bourgeoisie — and for the most part this nexus operates in unison — has the capacity or interest to develop the skills of an exceedingly young population let alone guarantee it a dignified income. And where young and old working people alike demonstrate enterprise so as to make ends meet, the response of the state is to suppress, confiscate, even destroy. Look no further than the treatment of Islamabad’s katchi abadi dwellers and street vendors in recent months. Containment of the political and economic freedoms of Pakistan’s teeming masses is what the militarised state apparatus knows best. But building container cities does not make acute contradictions disappear, they only magnify them. The writer teaches at Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad. Published in Dawn, September 25th, 2026

items.title: Delegate walkout, protests greet Netanyahu as he addresses UN General Assembly
items.description: NEW YORK: Dozens of delegates walked out of the UN General Assembly hall on Thursday as hundreds of protesters gathered outside the building while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu defended Tel Aviv’s actions amid growing international isolation, with elections looming that could threaten his political future. The walkout undersco­red the competing pressu­res facing Netanyahu, who is battling mounting criticism abroad over the Gaza conflict while campaigning for re-election at home ahead of an October 27 vote. On Thursday, Netanyahu delivered a combative address inside the General Assembly, where dozens of delegations walked out as he began speaking. The departing diplomats left large sections of the hall empty, creating a striking contrast with Netanyahu’s attempt to use the podium to present Israel’s case before the international community. Netanyahu responded by accusing his critics of hypocrisy and calling them “moral cowards.” He rejected allegations that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, saying Israel had prevented rather than committed genocide. He defended the country’s military actions in Gaza and elsewhere in the region. Delegates walk out of the General Assembly hall as Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arrives to address the 81st United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York City, US, September 24. — Reuters He also devoted a significant part of his speech to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, calling him “the antisemitic mayor of New York” and accusing him of spreading what Netanyahu described as lies about Israel. Mamdani, who had declined to join the street protests, responded after the speech. “Prime Minister Netanyahu used his speech to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitise his genocide of Palestinians,” Mamdani said. “No lie can change the fact that he remains the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity.” Mamdani previously said New York City lacked the authority to enforce the ICC warrant against Netanyahu, arguing that the appropriate authorities should carry it out. On Wednesday night, the mayor had hosted Palestinian families from Gaza at Gracie Mansion and planted an olive tree with them, saying: “May peace be our future.” The two scenes — protesters confronting his government’s policies on the streets and diplomats leaving the hall during his address — turned Netanyahu’s brief visit to New York into a day of parallel confrontation. Netanyahu’s stay had already been sharply shortened amid security concerns and expectations of protests. He arrived on Thursday morning, addressed the General Assembly and was scheduled to return to Israel the same evening rather than remain in New York overnight. Outside the UN, Jewish and Muslim activists, Palestinian supporters, human-rights campaigners, progressive Jewish groups, politicians, artists and musicians took part in separate demonstrations across Manhattan. Their messages varied, but opposition to Netanyahu’s government and Israel’s conduct of the Gaza war brought many of them into the streets at the same time. Demonstrators protest after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s address to the United Nations 81st General Assembly in New York City, U.S., September 24. — Reuters The protests also offered a visible glimpse of a generational shift in American attitudes toward Israel and Netanyahu. While support for Israel remains stronger among older Americans, younger Americans have become substantially more critical of the Israeli government. A Pew Research Centre survey conducted in May found that only 18 per cent of Americans aged 18 to 29 had a favourable view of the Israeli government, compared with 47pc among those aged 65 and older. Among the youngest Americans, 58pc expressed a favourable view of Palestinians, compared with 47pc among those 65 and older. That generational divide was visible on the streets of New York, where many of the demonstrators were young people, including students, activists, artists and younger politicians. The largest direct action outside the UN was organised by Jewish Voice for Peace, whose New York chapter brought hundreds of protesters to First Avenue and 39th Street. Demonstrators wearing matching white T-shirts sat in the roadway, chanting against Netanyahu and calling for an end to US support for Israel. For a while, protesters stood and sat in the street, linking arms and blocking traffic as police moved in to clear the roadway. The chants continued as officers began making arrests. At least 30 people, including actors and politicians, were arrested in the initial action. Police later said more than 100 protesters had been taken into custody. Among those detained were actors Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder, congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier and City Council member Chi Ossé. Musicians Julien Baker and Lucy Dacus and actor Elliott Page were also among the prominent figures taking part in the protests. Chelsea Manning, who joined the protest, said people outside government institutions needed ways to reject policies they regarded as imperialism, ethnic cleansing and genocide. “We can’t be in there. This is the closest that we can get,” she said. Manijeh Moradian, a university professor of Iranian and Jewish heritage who participated in the demonstration, said protesters had a responsibility to speak out against what was happening in Gaza with US support. Jewish groups divided The demonstrations also highlighted divisions within New York’s Jewish community. Progressive Jewish organisations, including New York Jewish Agenda, T’ruah, J Street, New Jewish Narrative, New Israel Fund and Partners for Progressive Israel, held a separate protest at Dag Hammarskjöld Plaza near the UN. “We are gathered here as American Jews, Israelis, New Yorkers, to say: You are not welcome here,” said Margo Hughes-Robinson, executive director of New York Jewish Agenda. T’ruah, a rabbinic human-rights organisation, called for a ceasefire and accountability for alleged war crimes. The organisers described their rally as an alternative for Jewish New Yorkers who opposed Netanyahu’s policies while retaining concern for Israel and Jewish security. They were confronted by pro-Netanyahu counter-protesters who blew whistles, used megaphones, chanted “Bibi”, and sang Israel’s national anthem. On the other side, the ultra-Orthodox anti-Zionist group Neturei Karta also demonstrated, arguing that opposition to Israel could not automatically be equated with antisemitism. Elsewhere, Jewish and Muslim demonstrators marched together towards the UN, while Palestinian activists and other organisations joined the broader mobilisation against Netanyahu. A city divided over Israel and Gaza As police loaded detained protesters onto buses outside the UN, Netanyahu was speaking inside a building protected by heavy security. Outside, demonstrators sought to challenge the Israeli prime minister’s account of the Gaza war; inside, diplomats expressed their opposition by leaving the chamber. The contrast was difficult to miss. For several hours on Thursday, New York’s streets and the UN General Assembly hall became parallel stages for the same international argument — one expressed through demonstrations and arrests outside, the other through a diplomatic boycott inside. And beneath both scenes was a changing American debate over Israel.

items.title: Climate change ultimate test of global equity – Mahama
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has described climate change as the ultimate test of global equity, calling for greater international commitment to climate justice and financing. Addressing the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, he said Africa contributed less than four per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions yet bore some of the heaviest burdens of climate devastation. President Mahama highlighted environmental challenges confronting the continent, including erratic rainfall, coastal erosion and desertification in the Sahel. “We face erratic rainfall, our coastal towns suffer relentless erosion, and our Sahelian regions face accelerating desertification. On 29 June this year, Ghana and coastal West Africa faced an unprecedented deluge,” he said. “Torrential rain, exceeding 160 millimetres, was dumped on seven coastal regions within 24 hours, resulting in 39 deaths and one still missing.” President Mahama said climate justice demanded that developed countries fulfilled their long-overdue financial commitments to countries most vulnerable to the impact of climate change. He said climate mitigation support must be operationalised through predictable, non-debt-creating grants rather than loans that further increase the debt burdens of fragile economies. President Mahama said recent extreme weather events offered clear warnings to those who had dismissed climate change as a hoax perpetrated by geopolitical opponents. “Melting glaciers, flash flooding, droughts, record-breaking heatwaves, brush fires, hurricanes and other extreme weather phenomena are unmistakable signals of an overburdened planet.” The President also called for greater international solidarity in addressing global health security, saying pathogens did not respect national borders or Gross Domestic Product (0GDP). He said the international community must build an equitable global health architecture that guaranteed regional manufacturing of vaccines and therapeutics, strengthened epidemic surveillance and financed resilient public health infrastructure across the Global South in accordance with the demands of the Accra Reset. President Mahama said that while African countries demanded greater representation at the United Nations and advocated a more equitable and just global order, African leaders also had a responsibility to put their own countries in order.

items.title: Education for society
items.description: NOTWITHSTANDING what might be going on in other countries, Pakistan has a real problem regarding violence against women. In the past few months alone, we have seen some horrendous incidents: ‘honour’ killings, marriage-of-choice killings, rapes, domestic violence, spousal violence and killings, abduction, rape and killing of minors, and violence against employees and staff. There is no dearth of reports from national and international bodies documenting the extent and severity of these issues. A couple of points stand out in these reports. One, we do not have good data on violence against women. Incidents are underreported, and there are no national registries or data sets of any sort. Most reported data comes from newspaper reporting, police case registrations, hotline reports, and so on. Two, though many reasons — poor laws and weak implementation, few protections, pathetic institutional arrangements, low reporting and conviction rates, delays, social and societal taboos, etc — are cited in these reports, a primary one is the impact of patriarchy: the control of men over society. Patriarchy shapes not only laws, norms, and expectations in this society; it also shapes responses: what she was wearing, why she was out at that time, why she was driving, and so on. Patriarchy is hard to spot, fight, and neutralise because it is embedded in almost every norm, rule, and law. Most societies have, historically and even today, used education to address society’s main issues. What it means to be educated has varied across societies and times, and one element (other than the ability to carry out tasks) has been the larger socialisation of the individual within society and the shaping of their values and norms. I want to pose the question: should we not be shaping our education to take on the issue of patriarchy and its impacts directly? Recently, my daughter started school as a fifth-grader in a public school in London. On the very first day, after introductions and other formalities, her teacher spent a couple of hours talking about the autism spectrum and notions of inclusion, expected behaviour, and what was not expected or what would not be tolerated. This came before any conversation about the English or math curriculum. This term, the heroes the class will be introduced to include Frida Kahlo, Mahatma Gandhi, Simone Biles, and a couple of human rights defenders from across the globe. We must address the most urgent social and cultural issues of our society through education. Every day when I walk her back from school and ask her about her day, she tells me about the book they have been reading in class, the documentary they saw, the discussions they had, etc. I have to ask specifically about her math, English and history lessons. They are there, and she is learning the subjects she is supposed to, but the school and her education are much more than that. This has been true every school day. It is about what she needs as a human being and a citizen; it is about values and the kind of society that needs to be there. Specific skills are just a small part of the ‘education’ she is getting. I went to some of the best schools in Lahore in the day. But when I landed in England for undergraduate studies, one of the first things I noticed, comparing my own educational experiences with those of my undergraduate peers from England, was that almost each one of my peers had been exposed to things I had not. All of them had good exposure to and knowledge of a major European language other than English. All of them had studied music for many years in their schools, and many could play one instrument fairly well or had a good understanding of it. Many of them had had singing lessons: some were good choir singers. So, language, music and singing. Their exposure to art was also more advanced than mine. The schools I attended focused much more on doing well in academic subjects and preparing for school-leaving examinations. Though schools, especially high-fee private schools, have changed a lot, including in Pakistan over the years, even the best of them today remain narrowly focused on subject understanding and examination performance. They do not give any importance to preparing citizens and human beings. Nor is there a demand for this from parents. In fact, the trend, at least in public schools, is the opposite. With clear evidence that most children in schools are not learning enough (77 per cent are ‘learning poor’), the focus has shifted to foundational learning to ensure students grasp the basics of language and math. But the danger is that this approach narrows the scope of education even more. We focus on only essential learning objectives and try to drill them into students. We teach these and test only these. We test only these, so we teach only these. Foundational learning is the flavour right now, and it is hard even to raise concerns about what this might mean for broader educational objectives. Education has always been about creating citizens and human beings who can take us forward. We must address the most pressing social and cultural issues of our society through education. If we do not, what is the point of education, and how else can we plan for a better society? Violence against women, in all its forms, and the grip of patriarchy on our society is exactly the kind of embedded issue that cannot be tackled through law alone and has to be challenged through education and with a sense of purpose. The sheer brutality of what we keep seeing should wake us up to the urgency with which this needs to be addressed. The writer is a senior research fellow at the Institute of Development and Economic Alternatives and an associate professor of economics at Lums. Published in Dawn, September 25th, 2026

items.title: Palestine in focus
items.description: ISRAEL’S barbaric violence in Gaza, as well as rampages by extremist Jewish settlers in the West Bank, have earned the Zionist state the opprobrium of several states during the ongoing UN General Assembly. While the impassioned speeches will not be enough to stop the violence against the Palestinian people, they do indicate that even some of Israel’s allies in the West are having a difficult time justifying its monstrous behaviour. French President Emmanuel Macron said the “spectacle” in Gaza should “shame us all”. He also highlighted the grim situation in the West Bank. Similarly, Turkish President Recep Erdogan termed Gaza an “inhumane … concentration camp”. At a separate meeting on the two-state solution, Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar slammed the Israeli “machinery of occupation”. At the same event, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said “time is running out” for the two-state solution. Perhaps the outgoing UN head was being overly optimistic — Israel has done all possible to ensure a viable Palestinian state does not emerge. Not too far from these meetings the Board of Peace was also holding a session, pledging $2.45bn for Gaza’s ‘recovery’. While the promise of these funds should be welcomed, the reality in the occupied Strip tempers any hopes for Gaza’s betterment. After all, since last year’s ceasefire Israel has murdered some 1,400 people in Gaza, mostly civilians, while Tel Aviv has refused to end its occupation of the Strip, even though Hamas agreed to give up its arms. Meanwhile, illegal settlements have exploded in the West Bank, with Jewish settlers growing more vicious in their attacks by the day. Therefore, throwing money at Gaza will do little if the Palestinians remain under siege, and the theft of their land continues. If conscientious members of the international community are serious about their concern for Palestine, they must back their talk with action. Israel must be held to account for its genocidal violence in Gaza, while settlers in the West Bank should be punished for their occupation of Palestinian land, and frequent physical attacks on Arabs. All illegal settlements need to be uprooted. Sadly, while calls for a two-state solution continue, the current Israeli regime — and whatever dispensation emerges after the coming elections in the Zionist state — will remain hell-bent on preventing a sovereign Palestinian state from emerging. Meanwhile, Israel’s most powerful foreign patron — the US — seems utterly uninterested in making Tel Aviv commit itself to the peace process. PR stunts under the Board of Peace are one thing; genuine pressure on Israel to end the occupation is another. Can the Palestinian people expect relief when such powerful actors remain committed to prolonging their suffering? Published in Dawn, September 25th, 2026

Senate body orders probe into ‘overcharging’ by telco
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Senate Standing Com­mittee on Information Technology and Tele­c­ommunication has constituted a subcommittee to investigate allegations that a leading telecom firm had charged customers Rs5.83 billion in excess of tariffs approved by the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA). The subcommittee, headed by Senator Dr Afnanullah Khan, will examine the alleged overcharging by Jazz and the regulatory action taken by the PTA in the matter. The decision was taken following a heated debate between PTA officials and representatives of the Auditor General of Pakistan (AGP). Committee Chairperson Senator Palwasha Khan intervened to pacify the situation when the PTA chairman threatened to resign if any allegation of corruption was levelled against him. Meanwhile, a Jazz spokesperson said the matter concerned two government entities and that Jazz would present its point of view if called before any relevant forum. The matter relates to the audit of the PTA for 2024. The audit objection stated that the telecom regulator had allowed a 15 per cent tariff increase for Jazz against a permissible limit of 3pc. The audit also suggested seeking the opinion of the Competition Commission of Pakistan (CCP) on the tariff policy. PTA Chairman retired Maj Gen Hafeezur Rehman questioned the proposal, saying that if tariffs were to be decided by the CCP, the PTA should not be held responsible for ensuring quality of service. “Let them take the whole responsibility,” he said. He maintained that the regulator had acted with complete transparency in allowing the 15pc tariff increase for Jazz and offered to have the matter subjected to a forensic audit. The PTA chairman categorically stated that he would resign if even one rupee of overcharging by the telecom operator was established in violation of the authority’s approved tariffs. He explained that the PTA examined mobile packages before their launch and monitored compliance with the approved tariff structure. However, audit officials had raised certain queries regarding the matter. Senator Palwasha Khan subsequently decided to constitute the subcommittee. It will examine the relevant tariff approvals, packages and billing details to determine whether customers were charged amounts beyond the rates approved by the regulator. Published in Dawn, September 25th, 2026

items.title: Full list: Atiku appoints Ibrahim-Imam, El-Rufai, Dino Melaye, others to ADC Campaign Council
items.description: ABUJA — Presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress, ADC, Atiku Abubakar, has approved the composition of his Presidential Campaign Council ahead of the 2027 general elections, naming Kashim Ibrahim-Imam as chairman and former Kaduna State Governor, Nasir El-Rufai, as deputy chairman. Read Also: Petrol Price Surge: FG gains, workers suffer — NLC; N70,000 wage inadequate – Keyamo The appointments were announced Thursday by Phrank Shaibu, Director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council and Senior Special Assistant on Public Communication to Atiku. Senator Austin Akobundu was named Director-General and Campaign Manager, with responsibility for coordinating the campaign’s operations and translating its strategy into action. According to Shaibu, the campaign structure comprises six Deputy Directors-General overseeing operational directorates, with 30 directors assigned specific responsibilities. Veteran journalist and publisher, Dele Momodu, will head the Media and Communications Directorate, while former Kogi West Senator, Dino Melaye, will lead Contact and Mobilisation. The Policy Team will be chaired by economist and banker Mohammed Hayatudeen, who will work with Professor Mohammed Sagagi and other members, including Professor Kingsley Moghalu. Former Edo State Governor and pioneer National Chairman of the All Progressives Congress, APC, John Oyegun, will chair the Campaign Advisory Board. Shaibu said the structure was deliberately designed as a lean, people-driven organisation in response to the economic challenges facing Nigerians. He said the campaign would focus on issues including the cost of living, unemployment, insecurity and declining purchasing power. “When families are struggling with food prices, transport costs and shrinking incomes, a campaign asking for their trust must show discipline in how it operates,” Shaibu said. He added that the structure was designed to give each directorate a clearly defined responsibility and ensure that appointees were accountable for results. “Our measure of success will be how clearly we address the cost of living, unemployment, insecurity and declining purchasing power—and how effectively we organise to make Nigeria affordable again,” he said. The campaign council is expected to coordinate Atiku’s presidential campaign activities nationwide ahead of the 2027 election. The ADC had earlier submitted Atiku’s name as its presidential candidate and former Rivers State governor, Rotimi Amaechi, as vice-presidential candidate to the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC.
